sources: MacAlister, R. A. Stewart. Lebor Gabála Érenn: The Book of the Taking of Ireland, Part 1. Dublin: Irish Texts Society, 1941, pp. 166–248.

text: According to the Book of Invasions, Cesair was the first settler of Ireland. The book was written after Ireland became Christian. The monks who wrote it wanted to show Ireland as a holy land. They joined Irish myth to biblical stories. In this account, Cesair was the granddaughter of the biblical Noah. She escaped the Flood by sailing from the Holy Land. Noah filled his boat with animals. Cesair filled hers with people, 50 women and three men. Cesair and her followers reached Ireland four days before the Flood. The waters never touched that land. Her route was not direct. She left from Meroe and sailed down the Nile. She passed the Caspian and Cimmerian seas and crossed the drowned Alps. It took nine days to reach Spain and nine more to reach Ireland. Cesair landed at Bantry Bay in County Cork. There she divided the land among the crew. With only three men, she made three groups, each with more than a dozen women and one man. Her father Bith and her brother Ladra died from excessive sexual exertion. The last man, Fintan mac Bóchra, fled the eager women. The women who accompanied Cesair bear names that echo ancestral mothers. They include German, Espa, Alba, Traige, and Gothiam. Their arrival reads as a microcosm of the world's people. Others, such as Banba and Búanann, echo the names of ancient Irish goddesses. Some scholars call Cesair a goddess of the land. She may be the daughter of the earth goddess Banba. She is also called Berba, the goddess of the River Barrow, and Heriu, a name near to Ériu. So Cesair may be a form of these divinities. The three men each took a primary bride. Fintan took Cesair, Bith took Bairrind, and Ladra took Banba. This makes Cesair a parallel to the goddess trio Banba, Fódla, and Ériu.

okr.objective: Cesair is the legendary first settler of Ireland in the Book of Invasions.
